title: Cache with TTL and Versioned Expiry — implement `put(key, value, ttl, now)` and `get(key, now)` where an entry is valid only while `now < expires_at`; a newer write replaces the old value AND expiry, so an old cleanup event must NOT delete a newer version of the same key (attach a version/sequence to each expiry record and verify it still matches before deleting) — lazy expiry gives O(1) per op; a heap for proactive cleanup adds O(log n) and stale-record management.
shortTitle: Cache with TTL and Versioned Expiry

s1_definition.profdef: A TTL cache stores each key with an expiry timestamp computed as the write time plus a time-to-live, and a read is valid only while the current time is strictly before that expiry. Because a newer write replaces both the value and the expiry, any proactive cleanup must carry a version or sequence number so a stale expiry event does not delete a newer version of the same key; lazy expiry checks validity on read in O(1), while an optional min-heap keyed on expiry enables proactive cleanup in O(log n) with stale-record skipping.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India caches a one-time password with a two-minute validity. Each OTP has a stamped expiry. If Rajesh requests a new OTP before the old one expires, the new one replaces the old value and its expiry. The danger is a cleanup robot holding an old reminder note that says "delete Rajesh's OTP at 10:02"; by then Rajesh has a fresh OTP valid until 10:05, so the robot must check the version number on its note against the current entry and, seeing a mismatch, leave the fresh OTP alone.
s1_definition.oneliner: Validate on read against the expiry, and stamp every expiry record with a version so a late cleanup never deletes a newer rewrite of the same key.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A TTL cache stores each key with an expiry timestamp computed as the write time plus a time-to-live, and a read is valid only while the current time is strictly before that expiry. Because a newer write replaces both the value and the expiry, any proactive cleanup must carry a version or sequence number so a stale expiry event does not delete a newer version of the same key; lazy expiry checks validity on read in O(1), while an optional min-heap keyed on expiry enables proactive cleanup in O(log n) with stale-record skipping.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India caches a one-time password with a two-minute validity. Each OTP has a stamped expiry. If Rajesh requests a new OTP before the old one expires, the new one replaces the old value and its expiry. The danger is a cleanup robot holding an old reminder note that says "delete Rajesh's OTP at 10:02"; by then Rajesh has a fresh OTP valid until 10:05, so the robot must check the version number on its note against the current entry and, seeing a mismatch, leave the fresh OTP alone.

**One line to remember:** Validate on read against the expiry, and stamp every expiry record with a version so a late cleanup never deletes a newer rewrite of the same key.

sections.s2_technical:
Each entry stores the value, an absolute expiry timestamp, and a version number that increments on every write to that key. The `put(key, value, ttl, now)` operation sets the value, sets expiry to now plus ttl, and bumps the version. The `get(key, now)` operation returns the value only if the entry exists and now is strictly less than expires_at; otherwise it reports a miss, and with lazy expiry it may also delete the stale entry on the spot. Lazy expiry alone makes every operation constant time because it just compares timestamps.

The versioning is the heart of correctness. If we also push expiry records into a min-heap ordered by expiry time for proactive cleanup, each heap record carries the key and the version it was created with. When the cleanup thread pops a record whose expiry time has passed, it must look up the current entry and compare versions: only if the entry still exists and its version equals the record's version does it delete the entry. If the versions differ, the key was rewritten after this record was created, so the record is stale and is discarded without touching the live entry.

The heap gives proactive cleanup so expired entries do not linger in memory, at a cost of O(log n) per push and pop, plus the management of stale records that are simply skipped. A senior nuance: using strictly-less-than for validity means an entry is dead exactly at its expiry instant, which must be consistent between get and cleanup. Another nuance is that without the version check, a delayed cleanup event would silently evict a freshly written value, causing a correctness bug that is very hard to reproduce.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India caches short-lived security tokens such as transfer authorization codes, each valid for a fixed number of seconds. A read must honor the expiry exactly so an expired code is never accepted.

This is exactly how TTL validation works. We compare the current time against the stored expiry and reject once it passes.

Problem 2 — A customer often refreshes a code before the old one expires, which rewrites the value and extends the expiry. A background cleanup scheduled for the old expiry must not wipe the refreshed code.

This is exactly why each expiry record carries a version, and cleanup deletes only when the version still matches the live entry, protecting newer rewrites.

The code will have an `Entry` holder with value, expiry, and version, a `TtlCache` with lazy `get`, versioned `put`, and a `proactiveCleanup` driven by a min-heap, and a runnable demo showing a refresh beating a stale cleanup with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a write at t=100 with ttl 60, a refresh at t=150, a stale cleanup at t=165, and reads.

Step 1: `put` at t=100 sets AUTH-SAV2001 to CODE-7788 with expiry 160 and version 1, and pushes an expiry record for (160, version 1) onto the heap.

Step 2: `get` at t=120 finds the entry and sees 120 is less than 160, so it returns CODE-7788.

Step 3: `put` at t=150 refreshes the key: version becomes 2, value becomes CODE-9900, expiry becomes 210, and a new expiry record for (210, version 2) is pushed. The old (160, version 1) record is still sitting in the heap.

Step 4: `proactiveCleanup(165)` pops the (160, version 1) record because 160 is at most 165. It looks up the live entry, whose version is now 2, which does not match version 1, so it skips the record and leaves the fresh entry intact. The (210, version 2) record stays in the heap because 210 is greater than 165.

Step 5: `get` at t=170 returns CODE-9900 because 170 is less than 210. `get` at t=215 sees 215 is not less than 210, lazily deletes the entry, and returns a miss.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 13:20:00 INFO    get @t=120 -> CODE-7788
2026-10-27 13:20:00 INFO    cleanup SKIP stale record AUTH-SAV2001 v=1 (live v=2)
2026-10-27 13:20:00 INFO    get @t=170 -> CODE-9900
2026-10-27 13:20:00 INFO    get @t=215 -> null
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A cache with time-to-live stores each key alongside an absolute expiry timestamp, computed as the write time plus the time-to-live, and a read is valid only while the current time is strictly before that expiry. Lazy expiry alone gives constant-time operations because a get simply compares the current time against the stored expiry and treats the entry as a miss, optionally deleting it, once the expiry has passed.

The subtle correctness problem appears when I add proactive cleanup so expired entries do not linger in memory. A newer write replaces both the value and the expiry of a key, but a cleanup event that was scheduled for the old expiry may still be pending. If that stale event fires and blindly deletes the key, it wipes out a freshly written value, which is a nasty, hard-to-reproduce bug. I solve it by attaching a version or sequence number to every write and to every expiry record. When the cleanup thread pops a record whose time has passed, it compares the record's version against the live entry's version and deletes only when they match; if they differ, the key was rewritten after the record was created, so the record is stale and is discarded without touching the live entry.

For the proactive side I use a min-heap ordered by expiry time, which costs logarithmic time per push and pop and requires simply skipping stale records, while the lazy read path stays constant time. I keep the validity comparison strictly less than consistently in both the read path and the cleanup path so an entry dies at exactly the same instant everywhere.

In my project at National Bank of India, we cached short-lived transfer authorization codes, and customers frequently refreshed a code before the old one expired, which rewrote the value and extended the expiry. The versioned expiry records ensured that a background cleanup scheduled for the old code never deleted the refreshed one, so a customer who legitimately renewed their code was never left stranded by a late cleanup event wiping their valid token.
